prompt: A processor is defined as:

options.text: The logic circuitry that responds to and processes the basic instructions that drive a computer
The set of instructions a programmer can give to a machine
The memory that holds the instructions
The interface between hardware and software

explanation: Logic circuitry that responds to and processes the basic instructions. It is hardware, not a set of instructions and not an interface.

why.a: Correct. Logic circuitry that responds to and processes the basic instructions.
why.b: Wrong. That is the instruction set, defined two lines later on the same slide.
why.c: Wrong. Instructions are stored in memory, but memory is not the processor.
why.d: Wrong. That is the ISA.

prompt: A processor is the {{1}} circuitry that responds to and processes the basic instructions that drive a computer.
explanation: Logic circuitry. The control unit and the ALU are both parts of it.

prompt: CPU instructions are numbers stored in memory.
explanation: They are, which is the stored program idea again: an instruction is just a bit pattern, and the instruction format slide shows one.

why.true: Correct. The deck states it plainly.
why.false: Wrong. An instruction such as ADD R1,R2 is stored as the number 11100011111110000001110000.

prompt: According to the RISC deck, an instruction set is:

options.text: A set of instructions a programmer can give to a machine to perform operations, specific to the CPU architecture
The logic circuitry that executes instructions
The numbers stored in memory during execution
The four basic operations of a processor

explanation: A set of instructions a programmer can give, and the deck adds that the instructions are specific to the CPU architecture, which is why software is tied to an ISA.

why.a: Correct. A set of instructions a programmer can give, and the deck adds that the instructions are specific to the CPU architecture, which is why software is tied to an ISA.
why.b: Wrong. That is the processor.
why.c: Wrong. Those are the instructions themselves, once loaded.
why.d: Wrong. Read, decode, execute, write back are the basic operations.

prompt: The instructions of a machine are specific to the CPU {{1}}.
explanation: Architecture. That is why an application compiled for x86 will not run on ARM.

prompt: Select the basic operations of a processor the deck lists.

options.text: Read instruction from memory
Decode
Execute
Write back
Branch

explanation: Four operations, and they line up with four of the five stages of the RISC pipeline: fetch, decode, execute, write back.

why.a: Correct, reading the instruction from memory is first.
why.b: Correct, decode is second.
why.c: Correct, execute is third.
why.d: Correct, write back closes the list.
why.e: Wrong. Branching is a kind of instruction, not one of the basic operations of executing any instruction.

prompt: The basic operations are: read instruction from memory, decode, execute, {{1}}.
explanation: Write back. In the five-stage pipeline a memory access stage sits between execute and write back.

prompt: What do CISC and RISC stand for?

options.text: Complex Instruction Set Computer and Reduced Instruction Set Computer
Compact Instruction Set Computer and Rapid Instruction Set Computer
Complex Integrated System Computer and Reduced Integrated System Computer
Controlled Instruction Sequence Computer and Registered Instruction Sequence Computer

explanation: Complex and Reduced. The words describe the instruction set, and the deck later stresses that reduced means reduced work per instruction rather than merely fewer instructions.

why.a: Correct. Complex and Reduced.
why.b: Wrong. Compact and Rapid are not the words.
why.c: Wrong. The middle words are Instruction Set.
why.d: Wrong on every word but Computer.

prompt: Over the years {{1}} major processor design philosophies emerged.
explanation: Two: CISC and RISC. They were developed to address different challenges in processor design and performance optimization.

prompt: During the 1960s and 1970s, what was the relationship between memory and processor hardware costs?

options.text: Memory was expensive while processor hardware was relatively cheap
Memory was cheap while processor hardware was expensive
Both were expensive
Both were cheap

explanation: Expensive memory, cheap hardware. That imbalance is the whole reason CISC made sense: spend transistors to save memory.

why.a: Correct. Expensive memory, cheap hardware.
why.b: Wrong, and reversed, which would have argued for RISC instead.
why.c: Wrong. The contrast between the two is the point.
why.d: Wrong, for the same reason.

prompt: During the {{1}} and 1970s memory was expensive while processor hardware was relatively {{2}}.
explanation: The 1960s, and cheap hardware. By the early 1980s the reasoning had reversed and RISC followed.

prompt: Engineers attempted to reduce program size by creating processors with powerful instructions capable of performing complex tasks in a single instruction, and this led to CISC.
explanation: That is the deck's account of CISC's origin: expensive memory made small programs valuable, so instructions were made to do more.

why.true: Correct, and it explains why the main objective of CISC is less code.
why.false: Wrong. This is the historical background the deck gives for CISC.

prompt: By the early 1980s researchers discovered that most programs:

options.text: Used only a small subset of the available instructions
Used almost every available instruction
Were limited by memory size
Spent most of their time in input and output

explanation: A small subset, which made the elaborate rest of a CISC instruction set look like wasted silicon.

why.a: Correct. A small subset, which made the elaborate rest of a CISC instruction set look like wasted silicon.
why.b: Wrong, and it would have been an argument for keeping CISC.
why.c: Wrong. Memory cost was the 1960s and 1970s problem.
why.d: Wrong. I/O is not what the observation was about.

prompt: By the early {{1}} researchers discovered that most programs used only a small subset of the available instructions.
explanation: The early 1980s, which is also when the first RISC projects were running at IBM, Stanford and UC-Berkeley.

prompt: Which observation about instruction timing led to RISC?

options.text: Complex instructions often required multiple clock cycles while simpler instructions executed much faster
All instructions took the same time
Simple instructions required multiple clock cycles
Clock speed could not be increased further

explanation: Complex instructions cost many cycles, simple ones few. Combined with the small subset finding, that is the entire case for RISC.

why.a: Correct. Complex instructions cost many cycles, simple ones few.
why.b: Wrong, and uniform timing is a RISC goal rather than a 1980s observation.
why.c: Wrong, and reversed.
why.d: Wrong. Clock speed is one of three performance factors but is not this observation.

prompt: The observation that simpler instructions could be executed much faster led to the development of RISC architectures.
explanation: It did, together with the finding that most programs use only a small subset of instructions.

why.true: Correct. The deck says this observation led to the development of RISC architectures.
why.false: Wrong. It is the conclusion drawn at the end of the historical background.

prompt: The first in-class question in the RISC and CISC deck asks:

options.text: Why were CISC architectures initially popular?
Why is pipelining more difficult in CISC processors?
Why do we not use only cache memory?
What is the primary focus of computer architecture?

explanation: It follows the historical background, and its answer slide comes next.

why.a: Correct. It follows the historical background, and its answer slide comes next.
why.b: Wrong. That is the second in-class question in this deck, much later.
why.c: Wrong. That belongs to the memory deck.
why.d: Wrong. That belongs to the introduction deck.

prompt: Why were CISC architectures initially popular?

options.text: Because memory was expensive, and CISC instructions could perform complex operations using fewer instructions, reducing program size
Because they were faster than RISC at the same clock rate
Because they pipelined more easily
Because they used fewer transistors

explanation: Expensive memory plus fewer instructions equals smaller programs. Every clause of the answer slide is doing work.

why.a: Correct. Expensive memory plus fewer instructions equals smaller programs.
why.b: Wrong. RISC achieves 2 to 4 times the performance at comparable clock rates.
why.c: Wrong, and the opposite: varying lengths and execution times make CISC harder to pipeline.
why.d: Wrong. Simple hardware and less chip space are RISC advantages.

prompt: CISC was initially popular because memory was {{1}}, and CISC instructions could perform complex operations using fewer instructions, thereby reducing program {{2}}.
explanation: Expensive memory, reduced program size. The cost of memory is what made size worth paying for.

prompt: CISC existed close to the beginning of general computing, when the earliest machines were programmed in assembly language and memory was slow and expensive.
explanation: That is the deck's framing. Assembly programming by hand is what made a hundred powerful instructions preferable to thousands of simple ones.

why.true: Correct, and it is the setting for the IBM instruction set decision on the same slide.
why.false: Wrong. This is how the deck opens its account of CISC.

prompt: IBM designed an instruction set to allow early programmers to easily program:

options.text: A hundred complex instructions rather than thousands of individual instructions
Thousands of complex instructions rather than a hundred individual ones
A hundred individual instructions rather than a thousand complex ones
Ten complex instructions rather than a hundred individual ones

explanation: A hundred complex against thousands of individual. The trade is fewer, richer instructions for the human writing them.

why.a: Correct. A hundred complex against thousands of individual.
why.b: Wrong, and reversed.
why.c: Wrong. The hundred are the complex ones.
why.d: Wrong figures. A hundred complex against thousands of individual.

prompt: {{1}} designed an instruction set to let early programmers write a hundred complex instructions rather than thousands of individual ones.
explanation: IBM, which also appears later on the other side of the argument, as the home of the IBM 801, one of the first RISC projects.

prompt: CISC was developed to make compiler development simpler. How?

options.text: It shifts most of the burden of generating machine instructions to the processor
It shifts most of the burden to the compiler
It removes the need for a compiler
It requires the compiler to schedule every instruction

explanation: The burden moves to the processor. RISC does the reverse, which is why the deck later says complexity is pushed to the compiler in RISC.

why.a: Correct. The burden moves to the processor.
why.b: Wrong, and that is the RISC position.
why.c: Wrong. A compiler is still needed; it is simply simpler.
why.d: Wrong. Instruction scheduling is a RISC compiler's job, and poor scheduling is a RISC disadvantage.

prompt: In CISC, most of the burden of generating machine instructions is shifted to the compiler.
explanation: The other way round. CISC shifts the burden to the processor, which is what makes compiler development simpler.

why.true: Wrong. Pushing complexity to the compiler is the RISC approach.
why.false: Correct. In CISC the processor carries the burden.

prompt: The deck's example of what a CISC processor has built in is:

options.text: The ability to calculate a square root
The ability to sort an array
The ability to draw a rectangle
The ability to translate an address

explanation: A square root, so the compiler does not have to emit a long sequence of machine instructions for it.

why.a: Correct. A square root, so the compiler does not have to emit a long sequence of machine instructions for it.
why.b: Wrong. Sorting is not mentioned.
why.c: Wrong. Rectangles belong to the vector graphics section.
why.d: Wrong. Address translation is the MMU's job.

prompt: Complex instruction set computing is a CPU design where single instructions can:

options.text: Execute several low-level operations, such as a load, an arithmetic operation and a store
Execute only one low-level operation each
Execute only register-to-register operations
Be decoded in a single cycle

explanation: Several low-level operations in one instruction, or multi-step operations, or addressing modes within single instructions.

why.a: Correct, and the deck names load, arithmetic and store as the example trio.
why.b: Wrong. That is closer to the RISC philosophy.
why.c: Wrong. Register-to-register only is the RISC restriction.
why.d: Wrong. Easy decoding is an important aspect of the RISC instruction format.

prompt: A CISC instruction may execute several low-level operations, such as a {{1}} from memory, an arithmetic operation, and a memory {{2}}.
explanation: Load, then arithmetic, then store, all inside one instruction. In RISC those would be three separate instructions.

prompt: CISC is called complex because of:

options.text: The complex work performed per instruction
The complexity of its compiler
The number of registers it has
The difficulty of manufacturing it

explanation: Work per instruction. It matches RISC being called reduced because of the reduction of work performed by an instruction.

why.a: Correct. Work per instruction.
why.b: Wrong. The CISC compiler is the simpler one.
why.c: Wrong. CISC has a small number of general purpose registers, but that is not where the name comes from.
why.d: Wrong. Manufacturing difficulty is not the reason given.

prompt: The CISC concept is to encode the {{1}} directly, as in add X and Y and put the result in Z.
explanation: The intention. You say what you want done, and the processor works out the steps.

prompt: The problem the deck identifies with CISC is that:

options.text: Some instructions take more time than others
All instructions take the same time
It has too many registers
Its instructions are too short

explanation: Uneven timing, which is exactly what makes pipelining hard: a pipeline wants every stage to take the same time.

why.a: Correct. Uneven timing, which is exactly what makes pipelining hard: a pipeline wants every stage to take the same time.
why.b: Wrong. Uniform timing is a RISC property and an advantage.
why.c: Wrong. CISC has a small number of general purpose registers.
why.d: Wrong. CISC instructions are variable in length, and often long.

prompt: In CISC, some instructions take more time than others.
explanation: They do, and the deck flags it as the problem. It comes back later as the reason CISC instructions are harder to pipeline.

why.true: Correct. The deck labels this the problem with CISC.
why.false: Wrong. Varying execution times are characteristic of CISC.

prompt: Which architectures does the deck give as examples of CISC?

options.text: x86 and s390
ARM and MIPS
IBM 801 and Berkeley RISC 1
DLX and MIPS

explanation: x86 and s390. All the other options are RISC machines.

why.a: Correct. X86 and s390.
why.b: Wrong. ARM is the smartphone RISC example and MIPS came out of Stanford's RISC project.
why.c: Wrong. Both are named as early RISC projects.
why.d: Wrong. Both are RISC.

prompt: CISC has a {{1}} number of general purpose registers.
explanation: Small. RISC leans the other way, since almost all its instructions work register to register and it needs plenty of them.

prompt: According to the deck, which devices typically use CISC and which use RISC?

options.text: Computers typically use CISC, while tablets, smartphones and other devices use RISC
Computers typically use RISC, while tablets and smartphones use CISC
Both use CISC
Both use RISC

explanation: Computers CISC, mobile devices RISC. The reason follows immediately: RISC is more efficient where cycles and power are in short supply.

why.a: Correct. Computers CISC, mobile devices RISC.
why.b: Wrong, and reversed.
why.c: Wrong. The slide draws a contrast.
why.d: Wrong, for the same reason.

prompt: Match each kind of device to the architecture the deck says it typically uses.
explanation: It lines up with the ISA example in the introduction deck, where mobile apps are built for the ARM-based processors in smartphones.

prompt: Why does the higher efficiency of RISC make it desirable in tablets and smartphones?

options.text: Because cycles and power are usually in short supply in these applications
Because memory is expensive in these applications
Because their compilers are simpler
Because they need variable-length instructions

explanation: Cycles and power. It is the same idea as battery life in the smartphone architecture example.

why.a: Correct. Cycles and power.
why.b: Wrong. Expensive memory is the 1960s and 1970s argument for CISC.
why.c: Wrong. RISC pushes complexity to the compiler, making it harder rather than simpler.
why.d: Wrong. Variable-length instructions are a CISC characteristic.

prompt: RISC is desirable where {{1}} and {{2}} are usually in short supply.
explanation: Cycles and power, the two things a battery-driven device cannot spare.

prompt: In CISC, instructions are executed by:

options.text: Microcode
Hardwired control
The compiler
The operating system

explanation: Microcode, and RISC uses hardwired control instead. That single contrast explains a great deal about both designs.

why.a: Correct. Microcode, and RISC uses hardwired control instead.
why.b: Wrong, and that is the RISC property.
why.c: Wrong. The compiler produces instructions; it does not execute them.
why.d: Wrong. The operating system is software running on the machine.

prompt: In CISC, instructions are executed by microcode.
explanation: They are, and the deck elsewhere adds that microcode control makes the CISC instruction set possible and flexible.

why.true: Correct. Microcode is the CISC mechanism; hardwired control is the RISC one.
why.false: Wrong. This is stated directly in the deck.

topic: why CISC is hard to pipeline
prompt: What about a CISC instruction set makes its instructions harder to pipeline?

options.text: It includes many instructions with different sizes and execution cycles
It includes too few instructions
Its instructions are all the same length
It has too many registers

explanation: Different sizes and different cycle counts. A pipeline works best when every instruction is the same shape and takes the same time.

why.a: Correct. Different sizes and different cycle counts.
why.b: Wrong. CISC has more instructions, typically 100 to 250.
why.c: Wrong, and uniform length is a RISC property that helps pipelining.
why.d: Wrong. CISC has a small number of general purpose registers.

topic: why CISC is hard to pipeline
prompt: A CISC instruction set typically includes many instructions with different {{1}} and execution {{2}}, which makes CISC instructions harder to pipeline.
explanation: Sizes and cycles. The answer slide to the second in-class question says the same thing in other words: varying lengths and execution times.

prompt: A CISC processor has a large number of instructions, typically:

options.text: From 100 to 250
From 5 to 20
From 250 to 500
From 50 to 100

explanation: 100 to 250 instructions. Do not confuse it with 5 to 20, which is the number of addressing modes on the very next line.

why.a: Correct. 100 to 250 instructions.
why.b: Wrong, and that is the addressing mode figure.
why.c: Wrong. The upper bound given is 250.
why.d: Wrong. The lower bound given is 100.

prompt: A CISC processor typically has from 100 to {{1}} instructions.
explanation: 250 is the top of the range, and 100 is the bottom.

prompt: A CISC processor has a large variety of addressing modes, typically:

options.text: 5 to 20 different modes
100 to 250 different modes
2 to 5 different modes
20 to 50 different modes

explanation: 5 to 20. The pair of figures on this slide, 100 to 250 instructions and 5 to 20 modes, are easily swapped under pressure.

why.a: Correct. 5 to 20.
why.b: Wrong, and that is the instruction count.
why.c: Wrong. The range given starts at 5 and ends at 20.
why.d: Wrong. 20 is the top of the range, not the bottom.

prompt: A CISC processor typically has from {{1}} to 250 instructions and from 5 to {{2}} addressing modes.
explanation: 100 to 250 instructions, 5 to 20 modes. Both ranges are worth memorising as a pair, because a question about one usually offers the other as a distractor.

prompt: A CISC processor includes some instructions that perform specialized tasks and are used infrequently.
explanation: It does, and that observation is what the 1980s researchers seized on: most programs use only a small subset of the available instructions.

why.true: Correct. It is one of the listed characteristics of CISC processors.
why.false: Wrong. The infrequently used specialized instructions are exactly what RISC set out to remove.

prompt: Select the characteristics of CISC processors from this list.

options.text: Variable-length instruction formats
Instructions that manipulate operands in memory
Uniform length instructions
Memory access limited to load and store

explanation: Variable length and memory operands are CISC. The other two are RISC properties, and they are the exact opposites.

why.a: Correct, variable-length instruction formats.
why.b: Correct, instructions that manipulate operands in memory.
why.c: Wrong. Uniform length and fixed format are RISC properties.
why.d: Wrong. Restricting memory access to load and store is the RISC rule.

prompt: CISC uses {{1}}-length instruction formats.
explanation: Variable. It saves memory, since a simple instruction need not be padded to the size of a complex one, but it complicates decoding and pipelining.

prompt: Among the properties of a CISC processor, how is its instruction set described?

options.text: Richer, some simple and some very complex, with instructions of a variable size
Simple and primitive, with instructions of a fixed size
Uniform in length and easy to decode
Limited to register-to-register operations

explanation: Richer and mixed, with variable size. Everything else in the list follows from that mixture.

why.a: Correct. Richer and mixed, with variable size.
why.b: Wrong. Simple primitive instructions is the first RISC property.
why.c: Wrong. Easy decoding is an important aspect of RISC.
why.d: Wrong. Register-to-register is the RISC restriction.

prompt: CISC has a {{1}} instruction set, some simple, some very complex.
explanation: Richer. Reduced is its opposite, and the R in RISC.

prompt: CISC instructions generally take:

options.text: More than 1 clock to execute
Exactly 1 clock to execute
Less than 1 clock to execute
A fixed 5 clocks to execute

explanation: More than one clock, against RISC's one instruction per clock cycle. That single number is behind most of the comparison table.

why.a: Correct. More than one clock, against RISC's one instruction per clock cycle.
why.b: Wrong, and that is the RISC property.
why.c: Wrong. No instruction takes less than a clock.
why.d: Wrong. The point is that CISC timing is not fixed.

prompt: CISC instructions generally take more than 1 clock to execute.
explanation: They do, which is why the comparison table says CISC is slower since an instruction can take more than 1 cycle.

why.true: Correct. It is the second listed property of a CISC processor.
why.false: Wrong. One instruction per clock is the RISC goal, not the CISC reality.

prompt: Among the listed properties of a CISC processor, what does the deck say about pipelining?

options.text: No pipelining
Pipelining, in five stages
Pipelining, but only for load and store
Pipelining is optional

explanation: No pipelining, listed as property 5. RISC lists pipelining as one of its own properties, so the two lists are mirror images.

why.a: Correct. No pipelining, listed as property 5.
why.b: Wrong. The five-stage pipeline is the RISC one.
why.c: Wrong. No such qualification is given.
why.d: Wrong. The property is stated flatly as no pipelining.

prompt: A CISC processor interfaces with memory in multiple mechanisms with {{1}} addressing modes.
explanation: Complex addressing modes. RISC has simple ones, and the comparison table states that contrast directly.

prompt: According to the listed properties, microcode control makes the CISC instruction set:

options.text: Possible and flexible
Faster and smaller
Fixed and uniform
Easier to pipeline

explanation: Possible and flexible. Without microcode, every complex instruction would have to be wired in by hand.

why.a: Correct. Possible and flexible.
why.b: Wrong. Microcode adds a layer of interpretation and does not make things faster.
why.c: Wrong. Flexibility is the opposite of fixed.
why.d: Wrong. CISC is harder to pipeline, not easier.

prompt: CISC works well with a simpler compiler.
explanation: It does, which is the seventh listed property and matches the earlier claim that CISC was developed to make compiler development simpler.

why.true: Correct. Work well with simpler compiler is listed as a CISC property.
why.false: Wrong. It is RISC that pushes complexity to the compiler.

prompt: The deck says microprogramming is as easy as assembly language to implement, and:

options.text: Much less expensive than hardwiring a control unit
Much more expensive than hardwiring a control unit
About the same cost as hardwiring
Only possible on RISC machines

explanation: Much less expensive than hardwiring. Cost, not speed, is the advantage claimed.

why.a: Correct. Much less expensive than hardwiring.
why.b: Wrong, and reversed.
why.c: Wrong. The deck asserts a clear cost advantage.
why.d: Wrong. Hardwired control is the RISC property; microprogramming belongs to CISC.

prompt: Microprogramming is much less expensive than {{1}} a control unit.
explanation: Hardwiring. RISC accepts that expense in exchange for speed.

prompt: As each CISC instruction became more capable, fewer instructions were needed for a task. What did that achieve?

options.text: More efficient use of the relatively slow main memory
More efficient use of the register file
Simpler pipelining
Fewer clock cycles per instruction

explanation: Fewer instructions means fewer instruction fetches, and fetches from slow memory were the bottleneck of the era.

why.a: Correct. Fewer instructions means fewer instruction fetches, and fetches from slow memory were the bottleneck of the era.
why.b: Wrong. CISC has few general purpose registers.
why.c: Wrong. Capable, variable instructions make pipelining harder.
why.d: Wrong. Complex instructions take more cycles each, not fewer.

prompt: Making each CISC instruction more capable meant fewer instructions were needed to implement a given task.
explanation: Fewer, more powerful instructions, which is the same trade the historical background describes as reducing program size.

why.true: Correct, and the benefit claimed is more efficient use of relatively slow main memory.
why.false: Wrong. This is one of the listed advantages of CISC.

prompt: Because micro-program instruction sets can be written to match the constructs of high-level languages:

options.text: The compiler does not have to be as complicated
The compiler has to be more complicated
No compiler is needed
The processor can be simpler

explanation: A simpler compiler, because the gap between the language and the machine is narrower.

why.a: Correct. A simpler compiler, because the gap between the language and the machine is narrower.
why.b: Wrong, and that is the RISC position.
why.c: Wrong. A compiler is still required.
why.d: Wrong. The complexity moves into the processor, not out of it.

prompt: Micro-program instruction sets can be written to match the constructs of {{1}} languages.
explanation: High-level languages. The closer the instruction set is to the language, the less translation the compiler has to do.

prompt: The first listed disadvantage of CISC is that complex instructions are:

options.text: Infrequently used by programmers and compilers
Frequently used but slow
Impossible to microcode
Too short to be useful

explanation: Infrequently used. All that silicon sits idle most of the time, which is precisely the 1980s finding.

why.a: Correct. Infrequently used.
why.b: Wrong. The complaint is that they are not used, not that they are used and slow.
why.c: Wrong. Microcode is what makes them possible.
why.d: Wrong. They are long, not short.

prompt: Complex instructions are {{1}} used by programmers and compilers.
explanation: Infrequently, which is the disadvantage that gave RISC its opening.

prompt: What does the deck say about memory references, loads and stores, in CISC?

options.text: They are slow and account for a significant fraction of all instructions
They are fast and rare
They are forbidden except in load and store instructions
They are handled entirely by microcode without touching memory

explanation: Slow and common, which is a bad combination. RISC's answer is to make them explicit and few.

why.a: Correct. Slow and common, which is a bad combination.
why.b: Wrong on both counts.
why.c: Wrong, and that is the RISC restriction, not a CISC disadvantage.
why.d: Wrong. Microcode sequences the work; it does not remove the memory access.

prompt: In CISC, memory references such as loads and stores account for a significant fraction of all instructions.
explanation: They do, and they are slow, which is why the deck lists this as a disadvantage.

why.true: Correct. Slow, and a significant fraction of all instructions.
why.false: Wrong. This is the second listed disadvantage of CISC.

prompt: The deck calls procedure and function calls a major CISC bottleneck. Why?

options.text: Because of passing arguments and storing and retrieving values in registers
Because they cannot be microcoded
Because they always miss in the cache
Because they require variable-length instructions

explanation: Argument passing and the saving and restoring of registers around the call. All of it is overhead that computes nothing.

why.a: Correct. Argument passing and the saving and restoring of registers around the call.
why.b: Wrong. Microcode is not the issue here.
why.c: Wrong. Cache behaviour is not what the slide names.
why.d: Wrong. Variable-length instructions are a separate characteristic.

prompt: Procedure and function calls are a major bottleneck: passing {{1}}, storing and retrieving values in {{2}}.
explanation: Arguments, and registers. Both halves are pure overhead around the useful work of the call.

prompt: The deck lists as a CISC disadvantage that the instruction set and chip become more complex with each generation of computers.
explanation: It does, and it is a compounding problem: every generation must keep the old instructions and add new ones.

why.true: Correct. It is the fourth listed disadvantage of CISC.
why.false: Wrong. The growth in complexity across generations is stated on the disadvantages slide.

prompt: How does the deck's CISC example multiply 5 by 10?

why.c: Wrong. That is the RISC philosophy example, breaking MULT A, B into four instructions.

prompt: The CISC example takes {{1}} instructions to multiply 5 by 10.
explanation: Three: two moves and a multiply. The RISC version needs a loop instead.

Intel, AMD and Motorola, in the late 80s
IBM alone, in the 1960s
Stanford and MIT, in the early 90s

prompt: The first RISC projects came from IBM, Stanford and UC-{{1}}.
explanation: UC-Berkeley, home of Berkeley RISC 1 and 2.
